sentence: Abstract—Influenza forecasts exist to support decisions, but the literature ranks them by mean squared error. We report an independent reproduction of MIFlu (Moon et al., IEEE JBHI 2025) on the CDC national influenza series (966 weekly rows, 7 channels, bit-identical to the author's file) and a 28-model benchmark the original work does not contain: 13 conventional forecasters, four LLM-based forecasters (MIFlu and three published ones), and 11 frozen large-language-model encoders. The reproduction lands within 4.5 % of the published four-horizon MSE mean (1.4995 against 1.4355) with a horizon-dependent sign: better at L=24 and L=36, worse at L=48 and L=60. On one common protocol (seeds 42/43/44; shared windows (W//16)*16 = 160/144/144/128) the accuracy champion is MIFlu (1.5574), ahead of PatchTST (1.6621) and NLinear (1.8716), and the spread across the roster is a factor of 3.6. On the epidemiological acceptance criterion of Kramer & Shaman (peak-timing error <= 1 week and peak-intensity error <= 25 % on ILITOTAL de-normalised to patient counts), NLinear and MIFlu each pass 4 of 16 cells, but differently: NLinear passes all four step-0 cells with a peak-intensity error of 3.2 %, while MIFlu's passes sit at 18.3-24.8 %, against the boundary. PatchTST passes none: its timing is the best in the study (mean 1.240 weeks) but its intensity error is 32.8 %. Accuracy and calibration are positively rank-correlated across all 28 arms (Spearman rho = +0.74), so MSE is a useful screen; but the frontier is ordered the other way round, and the pass indicator is negatively rank-correlated with MSE (rho = -0.43, p = 0.023). Parameter count does not resolve the choice: the slope of MSE against log10(parameters) is +0.1171 with R2 = 0.0223, the Pareto set is {NLinear, 2,520 parameters; PatchTST, 531,878 parameters}, and the 211x parameter cost buys an 11.2 % MSE difference that does not survive Holm correction over the 136 pairs (p = 0.117; with n = 12 no pair can). None of the 11 frozen encoders passes the criterion, and every one is worse than a decision tree. We argue that the acceptance criterion should be reported next to MSE, and that an MSE-sorted leaderboard can point a deployment decision the wrong way.
